title: UAE Retail T-Sukuk at 5.06%: what individual investors should know
author: Navvin S Bhalla
excerpt: The UAE's second sovereign retail sukuk offers a fixed 5.06% a year over five years from AED 1,000. How it works, what the first issuance showed, and the trade-offs to weigh before subscriptions close on 28 September.
body_html:
5.06%Annual profit rate, fixed
5 yearsTenor to maturity
AED 1,000Minimum subscription
23–28 SepSubscription window, 2026
Twice a yearProfit distributions
1 OctListing on Nasdaq Dubai

For most of the UAE's history, government debt has been an institutional market. Banks, pension funds and asset managers bought sovereign paper; individual savers did not. The Ministry of Finance's Sovereign Retail T-Sukuk Programme changes that, putting AED-denominated, government-backed Islamic securities within reach of anyone with AED 1,000 and a UAE investor account.

The second issuance, priced on 22 September, targets AED 50 million and pays a fixed 5.06% a year over five years, distributed every six months. It is open to UAE nationals and residents.

The two issuances side by side

First issuanceSecond issuance
Subscription window24–30 June 202623–28 September 2026
Annual profit rate4.30%5.06%
Tenor2 years5 years
Target sizeAED 50M (raised to AED 100M)AED 50M
MinimumAED 1,000AED 1,000
PayoutsSemi-annualSemi-annual
ListingNasdaq Dubai, 2 July 2026Nasdaq Dubai, 1 October 2026

The higher rate is not a sweetener. It is largely the price of time: investors committing capital for five years rather than two are paid a term premium, and the Ministry says the rate was set in line with prevailing market conditions.

What the first issuance told us

The June offering was the proof of concept, and demand was emphatic. Orders reached AED 445 million against a AED 50 million target, close to nine times oversubscribed, and the Ministry doubled the issue to AED 100 million.

The subscriber mix matters as much as the headline number. Investors placing AED 10,000 or less made up 76% of all subscribers, UAE nationals accounted for 72%, and investors under 25 together with women made up 45%. This was genuinely retail money, which is the point of the programme: building a domestic savings culture and a deeper AED capital market.

What the numbers look like

Because the rate is fixed and paid semi-annually, the cash flow is easy to model. Figures below are gross, assume the full amount is allocated and the sukuk is held to maturity, and do not reinvest payouts.

InvestedEvery six monthsPer yearOver five years
AED 1,000AED 25.30AED 50.60AED 253
AED 10,000AED 253AED 506AED 2,530
AED 50,000AED 1,265AED 2,530AED 12,650
AED 100,000AED 2,530AED 5,060AED 25,300

Why it appeals

Sovereign credit

The instrument is backed by the UAE Government, which places its credit risk at the lowest end of anything available to a UAE retail investor.

A low entry point

AED 1,000 is a fraction of what most fixed-income products demand for comparable yields, which is why small tickets dominated the first issuance.

Shariah compliance

Returns are structured as profit rather than interest, giving investors who avoid conventional bonds a clean sovereign option.

Predictable income

A fixed rate paid twice a year is simple to plan around, whether for household budgeting or a longer-term savings ladder.

The trade-offs

Low credit risk is not the same as no risk. Four things deserve attention before subscribing.

Selling early can mean a loss

Face value is repaid at maturity. Before then, the price on Nasdaq Dubai moves with interest rates. If rates rise over the next five years, a 5.06% sukuk becomes less attractive and may trade below what you paid. The protection only works if you can hold for the full term.

Liquidity can be thin

Market makers and liquidity providers support trading, but retail sukuk markets are young. Finding a buyer at a fair price mid-term may be slower or costlier than expected.

You may not get your full allocation

If this issuance is oversubscribed like the first, applications may be scaled back. Allocation is set for 29 September, with excess funds refunded on 30 September, so the uninvested remainder comes back as cash.

Inflation is the quiet risk

A fixed 5.06% protects you if deposit rates fall, but leaves you exposed if inflation runs above that level. Over five years, that is real purchasing power.

The operator's view. Treat this as the anchor of a savings plan, not the whole plan. It suits money you are confident you will not need for five years. For funds you may need sooner, the shorter first issuance on the secondary market or a laddered approach across future issuances may fit better.

How to subscribe

Subscriptions run until 28 September 2026 through the DFM eIPO platform, the iVestor app, the DFM app, and the digital channels of the receiving banks. Emirates NBD is lead receiving bank, with Emirates Islamic, Abu Dhabi Islamic Bank, Ajman Bank, Mashreq, Abu Dhabi Commercial Bank and First Abu Dhabi Bank participating. Units are credited to investor accounts after allocation and before listing.

This article is for general information only and does not constitute financial, investment or Shariah advice. OM4Biz is not a licensed financial adviser. Figures are drawn from public Ministry of Finance announcements as of 24 September 2026; confirm terms with the issuer or your bank before investing.

Sources

  • Ministry of Finance announcements via WAM, 2 July and 22 September 2026
  • Gulf News, Khaleej Times and The National coverage of both issuances

title: The Real Cost of Growing Old in the UAE: What Long-Term Expats Are Up Against
author: Navvin S Bhalla
excerpt: UAE retiree health cover averages USD 9,470 a year — among the priciest in the world — and long-term expats have no state pension, no portable social security, and residency tied to a financial threshold. What the numbers show, and how to plan around the gap.
body_html:
USD 9,470Avg. annual retiree health cover, UAE
Dh45,000Typical 65+ comprehensive plan/year
Dh1MProperty/savings threshold, retirement visa
Dh20,000Alternative monthly income threshold
0%Tax on pensions, dividends, investment returns
0UAE social security totalisation agreements with major sending countries

The UAE was built as a place people come to work, not a place they grow old. For decades that was the whole arrangement: earn, save, remit, and eventually leave. A growing share of its residents no longer fit that script. They arrived in their twenties, raised families here, built businesses here, and are now approaching retirement age with no state pension, no UAE social security record that travels home, and a healthcare bill that rises sharply with every year past sixty. The gap between what long-term expats have built here and what the system offers them in old age is widening, and it is worth understanding in detail — both as a personal planning problem and as an operating one for any UAE business with a tenured expat workforce.

How UAE retirement costs compare globally

Health insurance is the single biggest recurring cost of growing old in the UAE, and it is not close to the cheapest option available to a globally mobile retiree. A Pacific Prime study ranks the UAE the 14th most expensive country worldwide for international health insurance for retirees, at an average USD 9,470 a year. That is less than half the US figure (USD 23,231), but several multiples of the cost in the retirement destinations expats most often compare it to.

MarketTypical retiree health coverAnnualised (approx.)
United States—USD 23,231 / yr
UAE (average, all ages)—USD 9,470 / yr
UAE (comprehensive plan, 65+)—~ USD 12,250 / yr (Dh45,000)
Spain / Portugal~ €559 / mo~ USD 7,200 / yr
Mexico / Costa Rica~ €335 / mo~ USD 4,300 / yr

The spread matters more at 65+, where UAE premiums climb fastest. A comprehensive plan for a retiree in that bracket can reach Dh45,000 (about USD 12,250) a year — roughly the entire annual cost of comparable cover in Mexico or Costa Rica, doubled.

The trade-off: lifestyle against financial security

Almost no long-term expat frames the decision to stay as purely financial. It rarely is.

Why people stay

For residents who have spent twenty or thirty years here, the UAE is simply home — children were raised, careers were built, and the emotional ties run deeper than a posting. It is also a genuinely favourable place to hold wealth: there is no income tax on pensions, dividends or investment returns, which stretches whatever retirement savings a resident has accumulated. And the practical case is real too — world-class private healthcare infrastructure, a large English-speaking community, and among the highest personal safety standards anywhere.

What staying actually costs

Three structural gaps sit underneath the lifestyle case. First, there is no state pension: end-of-service gratuity, personal savings and whatever international pension a resident has kept up are the entire retirement system. Second, healthcare cost rises exactly when income typically falls, and for retirees on a fixed income it can become the deciding factor in whether to stay. Third, residency itself is conditional rather than guaranteed — it depends on clearing a financial threshold (Dh1 million in property or savings, or Dh20,000 in monthly income for the retirement visa route) and maintaining continuous health insurance without a lapse, which itself can jeopardise the visa.

The structural policy gap

The underlying issue is a mismatch of design and reality. UAE residency policy was built around temporary labour migration — workers arriving for a contract, then leaving. A large and growing share of the expat population no longer moves through the system that way; they are multi-generational, long-tenure residents whose working lives were spent entirely inside the UAE economy.

That population has no clean path to old-age protection. There is no mechanism to aggregate years of UAE residency with home-country pension contributions, because the UAE has no social security totalisation agreements with the countries that send it the most long-term residents, India among them. For many lower- and middle-income long-tenure workers, the honest retirement plan is simply to keep working as long as possible — not for income alone, but because employment is what keeps the visa, and the visa is what keeps the healthcare access, active.

The practical effect is a transfer of responsibility. Decades of economic contribution happen inside the UAE; the cost of old age, when it arrives, is quietly pushed back onto the home country or onto whatever the individual managed to save privately.

A practical path forward

Plan from year one, not year fifty-five

Retirement planning has to be treated as a personal responsibility from the first UAE payslip, not something addressed once retirement is a few years away. The tax-free structure rewards early, disciplined saving far more than it rewards catching up late.

Build savings that don't depend on residency

International pension schemes and investments held outside the UAE system protect income regardless of where a resident eventually retires — UAE, home country, or a third location. Portability is the entire point; a plan that only works if the visa holds is not a plan.

Budget for healthcare as a core line item, not a surprise

Health insurance cost in the UAE does not rise gently with age — it climbs sharply after sixty. Modelling that increase into a retirement budget in advance, rather than discovering it at renewal time, is the difference between a manageable plan and a forced decision to leave.

The operator's view. This is not only a personal-finance story — it is a workforce-retention one. Any UAE employer with long-tenured expat staff is, in effect, competing against this exact gap every time a senior employee starts doing the arithmetic on staying past fifty. Structuring end-of-service benefits, voluntary savings plans and senior-tier health cover deliberately — rather than leaving them at statutory minimums — is one of the more underused levers UAE employers have for retaining the institutional knowledge that a decade-plus employee actually represents.

This article is for general information only and does not constitute financial, tax, immigration or insurance advice. OM4Biz is not a licensed financial adviser. Figures are drawn from third-party market research (including Pacific Prime's international health insurance cost reporting) and publicly available UAE residency and retirement-visa criteria current as of September 2026; confirm current thresholds and costs with a licensed adviser or the relevant UAE federal authority before making a retirement or visa decision.

Sources

  • Pacific Prime — Cost of International Health Insurance report (retiree health cover rankings and averages)
  • UAE Federal Authority for Identity, Citizenship, Customs & Port Security — retirement visa eligibility criteria
  • Regional reporting on long-term expat retirement experiences and the UAE's social security agreement landscape

title: A Valid Tax Invoice Is No Longer Enough: What FTA Decision No. 13 Means for UAE Input VAT Recovery
author: Navvin S Bhalla
excerpt: From 1 October 2026, FTA Decision No. 13 requires UAE businesses to verify suppliers and transactions before recovering input VAT — a valid tax invoice alone is no longer sufficient. What the rules require, the AED 10,000/100,000/375,000 thresholds, and what it means for procurement and AP going forward.
body_html:
1 Oct 2026Decision No. 13 takes effect
AED 10,000Per-supply exemption threshold
AED 100,00012-mo. spend cap on that exemption
AED 375,000Enhanced due-diligence trigger
12 monthsMandatory supplier re-verification cycle
Art. 54 bisVAT Law provision this Decision implements

From Thursday, 1 October 2026, UAE taxable persons must perform and document specific supplier and transaction checks before deducting input VAT. The requirement comes from Federal Tax Authority (FTA) Decision No. 13 of 2026, issued on 22 July 2026, which gives operational content to Article 54 bis of the VAT Law — a provision inserted by Federal Decree-Law No. 16 of 2025 and in force since 1 January 2026.

The practical shift: input VAT recovery has always required a valid tax invoice. It now also requires an evidence file showing a business knew who it was dealing with and that the deal made commercial sense.

The legal logic: “knew or should have known”

Article 54 bis lets the FTA deny input VAT where a supply, or any link in its supply chain, is connected to tax evasion and the recipient either knew of that connection — denial is then mandatory — or should have known, in which case denial is discretionary.

Decision No. 13 defines what “should have known” means in practice: a business that has not carried out the prescribed verification is treated as having been required to be aware. Skipping the checks removes the “we had no way of knowing” defence.

Two points worth stating plainly: failing the checks is not an allegation of evasion — it goes only to whether a claim can be defended if evasion exists somewhere in the chain. And the rule bites only where evasion is actually present in the chain, but a business will not control whether it is, which is exactly why the file matters.

What the Decision requires

1. Supplier verification

Completed the first time a business deals with a supplier and repeated at least every 12 months.

  • Company suppliers: verify incorporation and registration details, and the identity and authority of the director, agent or representative.
  • Individual suppliers: verify valid identification and the person’s identity.
  • Physical presence: confirm the supplier has a genuine place of business consistent with its licensed activity.
  • Risk indicators: screen for frequent changes of address or management, and for transaction volumes out of line with the supplier’s history.

2. Transaction (supply) verification

Before deducting input VAT, a business must be able to show:

  • Commercial rationale, including why any intermediary is in the chain.
  • Market-aligned pricing, and that the supply falls within the supplier’s licensed activities.
  • Authenticity and origin of goods where relevant.
  • Justified payment arrangements — cash, third-party payments and payments to foreign bank accounts need a documented commercial reason, with electronic payment the expected default.

Three tiers of verification

LevelTrigger (rolling 12 months)What applies
Limited exceptionIndividual supply below AED 10,000 (excl. VAT)Not required — unless cumulative purchases from that supplier exceed AED 100,000
StandardAED 10,000 – 375,000Full supplier and transaction due diligence
EnhancedAbove AED 375,000Standard checks plus written UAE bank account confirmation and a review of public information and supplier reputation

The AED 10,000 exception is tested per individual supply, not on total annual purchases. A vendor bought from repeatedly in small amounts can still lose the exception once cumulative spend crosses AED 100,000. The AED 375,000 enhanced-tier trigger is forward-looking as well as historical: it applies if a supplier’s transactions exceeded that amount over the past 12 months, or are expected to over the next 12.

Implications going forward

Vendor onboarding becomes a tax control

Procurement and finance can no longer treat supplier setup as an administrative step. A vendor file is now part of a business’s VAT position.

The existing supplier base is exposed from day one

Every active vendor above the exception needs a verification file. Expect a backfill exercise prioritised by spend — enhanced-tier suppliers first, then standard, then the long tail.

Rolling-spend monitoring has to be systematic

Because the AED 100,000 and AED 375,000 triggers look forward as well as back, spreadsheets will struggle. ERP or AP tooling should flag a vendor crossing a threshold before the invoice is claimed, not after.

Payment behaviour is now audit evidence

Cash payments, third-party settlements and offshore transfers each need a written justification. Businesses with agent-based payments — trading, logistics, construction — should review their patterns first.

The annual refresh is a permanent compliance cycle

Verification decays after 12 months. Someone needs to own the calendar, not just the initial rollout.

Intermediaries face more scrutiny

Where a supplier sits between a business and the real source of supply, a commercial explanation for its role is required. Long or opaque chains carry more risk.

The cost of gaps is concentrated and hard to repair later

Denied input VAT is a direct hit to margin and can come with reassessment and penalties. Because the Decision applies at the point of deduction, gaps found in an audit are difficult to fix retroactively.

The operator’s view. This Decision doesn’t change the VAT rate or who can claim — it changes what a business must be able to prove when it does. Businesses that fold supplier due diligence into existing procurement and accounts-payable workflows will absorb this quietly. Those that treat it as a one-off compliance exercise before 1 October, without a system for the ongoing 12-month refresh and threshold monitoring, will find themselves exposed again within a year. Documentation retained alongside the invoice — not diligence performed but unrecorded — is what actually protects a claim at audit.

A practical readiness checklist

  • Adopt a written policy defining who performs, reviews and approves supplier verification.
  • Segment the vendor master by rolling 12-month spend against the AED 10,000 / 100,000 / 375,000 markers.
  • Build a standard verification pack: trade licence, incorporation documents, authorised signatory details, proof of premises, VAT registration status — plus bank confirmation and a reputation review for enhanced-tier suppliers.
  • Add a transaction-level gate to the AP process covering rationale, pricing benchmark, licence-scope check and payment-method justification.
  • Automate threshold alerts and 12-month refresh reminders in the ERP or AP system.
  • Train procurement and AP teams so red flags — address changes, unusual volumes, third-party payment requests — get escalated rather than absorbed.
  • Retain every verification record alongside the invoice, in a form that can be produced quickly at audit.

This article is for general information only and does not constitute tax or legal advice. OM4Biz is not a licensed tax adviser. Application depends on each business’s facts; consult a qualified VAT adviser and refer to the FTA’s published text of Decision No. 13 of 2026 before acting.

Sources

  • FTA Decision No. 13 of 2026, via PwC Middle East tax alert
  • EY Global Tax News, 26 August 2026
  • VATupdate.com coverage, August–September 2026
  • Khaleej Times business coverage

title: Petrol at AED 4.28: what 19 years of fuel prices teach operators about cost control
author: Navvin S Bhalla
excerpt: Special 95 has risen from AED 1.67 to AED 4.28 since 2007, about three times the pace of general inflation. What changed, and how to test whether a rising cost actually hurt your margins.
body_html:
+156%Special 95, Oct 2007 to Oct 2026
AED 1.67Per litre, October 2007
AED 4.28Per litre, October 2026
~5.1%Compound annual growth
~45–50%Estimated headline CPI, same period

I arrived in the UAE in 2007. That October, Special 95 cost AED 1.67 per litre. In October 2026 it is AED 4.28, an increase of 156%, or about 5.1% a year, compounded.

After 25+ years running BPO/KPO operations, contact centre governance and multi-entity businesses, I have learned that the costs that hurt a business are rarely the big line items everyone watches. They are the ones that stopped behaving the way we budgeted for. Petrol is a good case study.

The numbers

Oct 2007Oct 2026Change
Special 95 (AED per litre)1.674.28+156%
Cost of 60 litresAED 100AED 257+AED 157
Compound annual growth~5.1%

The AED 4.28 includes 5% VAT. Without VAT the price is about AED 4.08, still +144% on 2007, so VAT explains only a small part of the rise.

Petrol against general inflation

UAE headline inflation over the same period was uneven:

  • 2008: 12.3%, the highest on record, driven by the property and construction boom
  • 2019 to 2021: -1.9%, -2.1% and 0.2%, as rents fell
  • 2022: 5.3%, on global energy and food costs
  • 2023 to 2025: 1.6%, 1.7% and 1.3%

Compounding annual CPI figures gives an estimate of roughly 45 to 50% cumulative inflation since 2007, or about 2% a year. Petrol rose 156% over the same period, at roughly three times the pace of general prices.

What changed

1. Deregulation (August 2015)

Before 2015, pump prices were administered, so fuel behaved like a fixed cost. Since then, prices are set monthly from global benchmarks plus distribution margins. Fuel went from a managed price to a market price.

2. VAT (January 2018)

The 5% VAT added a step-up, but as shown above it is a minor part of the story.

3. Global energy volatility

The pump price now follows crude oil, refining margins and regional geopolitics, and it reaches a Dubai budget within weeks.

Did petrol really hurt a business? Test it against revenue

A fuel bill rising 2.5x only hurts if revenue did not keep pace. The right test is fuel as a share of revenue.

Take a hypothetical operation with 20 vehicles (staff transport, deliveries or field teams), each using 300 litres a month. This is an illustrative scenario, not a client case.

  • 2007: 6,000 L x AED 1.67 = AED 10,020 a month
  • Today: 6,000 L x AED 4.28 = AED 25,680 a month

Assume the fleet supported AED 500,000 a month of revenue in 2007, so fuel was 2.0% of revenue. What happens next depends on revenue growth:

Revenue growth, 2007 to 2026Revenue todayFuel as % of revenueEffect on margin
+50% (about headline inflation)AED 750,0003.4%-1.4 pts
+100%AED 1,000,0002.6%-0.6 pts
+156% (matches petrol)AED 1,280,0002.0%Neutral
+200%AED 1,500,0001.7%+0.3 pts

The 2% starting share and the growth scenarios are assumptions for illustration.

To stay neutral, revenue has to grow about 5.1% a year, in line with petrol. A business whose pricing merely followed general inflation lost about 1.4 margin points on this one line, without any operational failure.

Where it bites hardest:

  • Fixed-rate contracts and long-term client agreements with no fuel or escalation clause
  • Per-seat or per-hour pricing where transport is a hidden cost
  • Thin-margin operations, where 1.4 points is a large share of profit

Where it is absorbed:

  • Fuel is a small share of the cost base
  • Contracts have escalation clauses or annual repricing
  • Efficiency gains (routing, pooling, hybrid rosters) cut litres while revenue grew

Petrol outran general prices, and businesses whose revenue grew below about 5% a year fell behind on this cost line. How much it hurt depended on how large fuel was in their cost base.

Five lessons for operators

  1. Separate fixed costs from market-linked ones. Fuel, freight and energy follow global benchmarks and belong in a variable-cost model, not a flat annual figure.
  2. Stress-test your forecasts. Budget at a base price and test at +15% and +30%. Monthly repricing makes this straightforward.
  3. Track cost as a share of revenue. An absolute cost that looks alarming may be harmless, and a modest one may be quietly eroding margin.
  4. Cut the litres, not only the price. Route planning, shift scheduling, staff transport pooling and hybrid rosters reduce consumption. In contact centres, capacity planning that reduces transport hours reduces fuel cost directly.
  5. Re-check EV and hybrid economics. At AED 4.28, fleet electrification looks very different from how it did in 2007.

The operator's view. Costs don't need to spike to hurt you; they only need to drift unnoticed. Good operations governance means knowing which of your costs are managed and which are market-driven, and checking each against revenue before the market forces you to.

This article is for general information only. Petrol prices are as announced for October 2026. The cumulative CPI figure is an estimate compounded from annual inflation rates and should be read as approximate. The fleet example uses assumed figures for illustration and is not a client case.

Sources

  • UAE Ministry of Energy fuel price announcements, October 2007 and October 2026
  • Trading Economics, UAE inflation and Dubai CPI series
  • UAE Inflation Rate Calculator, annual CPI history
